stem: A 7-month-old is febrile, drowsy and irritable, with a bulging fontanelle and repeated vomiting. HR is 178/min, CRT 5 seconds, and BP 72/38 mmHg. The paediatric team suspects bacterial meningitis.
ask: Which next action is MOST appropriate?
options: Perform lumbar puncture immediately before IV access despite poor perfusion.
Begin sepsis resuscitation and empirical IV antibiotics promptly, deferring LP until stable.
Give oral antibiotics and review in primary care tomorrow.
Wait for a CT brain to prove meningitis before therapy.
Give acetaminophen alone and repeat fontanelle examination after an hour.
explanations: Shock makes LP unsafe as the first step and delays lifesaving antibiotics.
Correct: shock and possible meningitis demand ABC support and time-critical antibiotics.
Impaired consciousness and hypoperfusion require hospital admission and IV treatment.
Routine CT does not establish bacterial meningitis, and imaging delays treatment.
Antipyretic does not treat serious bacterial infection or shock.
pearl: Shock or impaired consciousness in suspected meningitis changes the priority from 'LP first' to stabilisation and antibiotics first.
pivot: Stable children without LP contraindications should have CSF collected promptly when this won't delay antimicrobial therapy.

steps: Stabilise
ABCDE, age-appropriate airway support, IV/IO access, glucose and reassessed resuscitation fluids.
Antibiotics
Obtain blood cultures if rapid, then give empirical meningitis IV antibiotics per local age/resistance policy.
Investigate safely
LP when haemodynamics/neurologic status permits; consider imaging only for indications.
Monitor
PICU input for shock, seizures and raised ICP concerns.
management.safety: Do not force LP in haemodynamic shock or with unsafe neurological signs.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

stem: A 3-month-old with large VSD sweats during feeds, breathes rapidly and has weight gain below expected. Examination shows tachycardia, hepatomegaly and a loud pansystolic murmur. Saturation is 97% on room air.
ask: Which management plan is MOST appropriate?
options: Give continuous oxygen as definitive treatment of the left-to-right shunt.
Treat heart failure symptoms, optimise nutrition and refer paediatric cardiology for defect closure planning.
Reassure that every VSD closes spontaneously without clinical follow-up.
Give prostaglandin E1 as standard treatment for all VSDs.
Start beta blockers at high doses without cardiac evaluation.
explanations: Oxygen does not remove shunt volume load and may increase pulmonary blood flow.
Correct: symptomatic large VSD needs diuretic/nutritional support and timely intervention assessment.
Small VSDs may close; symptomatic large defects risk failure to thrive/pulmonary hypertension.
Most isolated VSDs are not duct-dependent lesions.
Non-individualised therapy may worsen haemodynamics; anatomy and severity need specialist review.
pearl: A large left-to-right shunt becomes symptomatic after pulmonary vascular resistance falls in infancy.
pivot: A tiny restrictive VSD with no growth or haemodynamic problem may need surveillance only.

steps: Assess
Work of breathing, feed volume, weight, hepatomegaly and echo anatomy/shunt severity.
Support
Careful diuretics when congested and concentrated feeds/dietetic support.
Plan definitive care
Paediatric cardiology assessment for closure timing and pulmonary hypertension risk.
Monitor
Growth, infections, electrolytes and signs of worsening heart failure.
management.safety: Oxygen is not automatically helpful in a child whose main problem is excessive pulmonary blood flow.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

stem: A 6-week-old has inspiratory stridor that is louder when supine and during feeding but quietens when prone or upright. He is afebrile, SpO2 99%, feeding adequately and gaining weight. No cyanotic events.
options: Arrange urgent endotracheal intubation because all infant stridor is an airway emergency.
Explain likely laryngomalacia, arrange clinical/ENT follow-up and monitor feeding, weight and danger signs.
Give broad IV antibiotics for suspected epiglottitis.
Use routine oral steroid therapy until the stridor disappears.
Perform flexible bronchoscopy urgently under sedation without clinical risk assessment.
explanations: Stable typical laryngomalacia usually does not require intubation.
Correct: positional early-infant stridor with normal growth is often benign but needs surveillance.
Chronic positional stridor without fever/toxicity does not suggest epiglottitis.
Steroids are not typical treatment for uncomplicated laryngomalacia.
Airway endoscopy may be useful when severe/atypical, but routine sedation is not required in a thriving infant.
pearl: Laryngomalacia stridor worsens supine/feeding and improves upright; poor weight gain or apnoea changes urgency.
pivot: Stridor at rest with drooling and acute febrile toxicity signals dangerous supraglottic infection instead.

steps: Assess severity
Feeding, cyanosis, apnoea, recession, growth and associated anomalies.
Support
Feeding posture, reflux assessment if clinically significant, avoid unnecessary treatment.
Refer selectively
ENT flexible nasendoscopy for confirmation/atypical features; specialist surgery for severe failure to thrive or hypoxaemia.
Safety-net
Return for apnoea, persistent retractions, blue spells or faltering growth.
management.safety: Do not dismiss worsening inspiratory obstruction solely because oxygen saturation was once normal.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

stem: A 7-week-old has frequent paroxysms of cough ending in brief apnoea and cyanosis. Immunisations are not yet complete. An older sibling has a prolonged cough. The infant is afebrile, but SpO2 drops during episodes.
options: Reassure because lack of fever excludes serious respiratory infection.
Admit for apnoea monitoring, send pertussis testing and start an appropriate macrolide with infection-control advice.
Give oral codeine to suppress cough and discharge.
Give IV corticosteroids alone for presumed croup.
Wait for the classical whoop before undertaking any treatment.
explanations: Pertussis often causes minimal fever and can present with apnoea in young infants.
Correct: pertussis in a young infant warrants monitoring, early therapy and contact management.
Codeine is unsafe in infants and does not treat pertussis.
No stridor/barking cough, and steroids are not the primary pertussis treatment.
Infants may have apnoea without whoop; waiting increases risk.
pearl: Pertussis in young infants may cause apnoea rather than a characteristic whoop; protect high-risk household contacts.
pivot: An older immunised child with mild prolonged cough may receive outpatient evaluation depending on severity.

steps: Protect breathing
Hospital assessment, saturation and apnoea monitoring; airway support if episodes.
Test/treat
Nasopharyngeal PCR when indicated and macrolide per infant age/local dosing.
Infection control
Droplet precautions and public-health notification/contact prophylaxis as indicated.
Follow
Feeding, hydration and family vaccination/cocooning advice.
management.safety: Do not prescribe unsafe cough suppressants or assume afebrile illness is benign.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

stem: A 15-month-old with acute gastroenteritis is lethargic, pulse 168/min, CRT 6 seconds, sunken eyes and no wet nappy for 10 hours. BP is 74/38 mmHg. She can only take small sips.
options: Offer oral rehydration solution only and wait several hours for circulatory recovery.
Begin IV/IO isotonic crystalloid bolus under paediatric shock protocol with close reassessment, then plan deficit replacement.
Give hypotonic IV fluid rapidly without electrolyte monitoring.
Give IV furosemide for low urine output.
Give loperamide to stop diarrhoea immediately.
explanations: Shock with poor perfusion needs urgent parenteral resuscitation first.
Correct: treat hypovolaemic shock first, then maintenance and losses.
Hypotonic large boluses can worsen hyponatraemia and cerebral injury.
Oliguria is from low perfusion; diuresis worsens shock.
Antimotility agents are generally avoided in young children and do not restore circulation.
pearl: Capillary refill, mental state, pulse quality and urine output define dehydration severity beyond the number of stools.
pivot: In a well-perfused child with mild/moderate dehydration, oral/NG rehydration is usually preferred.

steps: Resuscitate
ABCDE, glucose and isotonic fluid boluses with frequent reassessment for overload.
Correct deficits
Electrolytes, glucose and weight-based maintenance/deficit plan after shock reversal.
Resume enteral
Oral/NG rehydration and feeds as tolerated, replace ongoing losses.
Monitor
Urine output, electrolytes, perfusion and stool warning signs.
management.safety: Avoid treating a septic child as 'dehydration only' without checking for infection and alternate causes.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

stem: An 8-year-old has dozens of brief daily episodes of abrupt staring lasting 8 seconds. She stops talking mid-sentence and resumes immediately without confusion. Provoked hyperventilation triggers a spell; EEG shows 3-Hz generalised spike-and-wave.
ask: Which treatment is MOST appropriate for uncomplicated childhood absence epilepsy?
options: Ethosuximide as a first-line antiseizure drug after paediatric neurology evaluation.
Carbamazepine because all focal-looking spells require sodium-channel blockade.
Diazepam prophylaxis every morning for years.
No treatment because episodes are always behaviour and harmless.
Immediate neurosurgical resection of temporal lobe.
explanations: Correct: typical isolated absence seizures often respond to ethosuximide.
Carbamazepine may aggravate generalised absence seizures.
Daily benzodiazepines cause tolerance and are not standard first-line maintenance for typical absence.
Frequent EEG-confirmed seizures impair learning and carry safety implications.
Typical generalised absence epilepsy is not a focal surgical lesion.
pearl: Typical absence seizures are brief, frequent, no postictal state and 3-Hz spike-and-wave EEG.
pivot: If generalised tonic–clonic seizures coexist, valproate or other broad-spectrum treatment may be favoured by specialist (with reproductive safety considerations).

steps: Confirm
Detailed witness history, school impact, hyperventilation and specialist EEG review.
Treat
Ethosuximide when absence-only, dose titration and adverse-effect monitoring per neurology.
Educate
Water safety, school recognition and seizure first aid.
Follow
Document frequency and EEG/clinical response; reassess for other seizure types.
management.safety: Medication choice changes if the child also has convulsive seizures.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

stem: A 10-year-old with prior untreated sore throat develops migratory large-joint arthritis, fever and a new apical pansystolic murmur four weeks later. ESR is high, antistreptolysin O titre is elevated and echocardiography shows mitral regurgitation.
options: Give NSAID alone because arthritis will resolve and cardiac treatment is unnecessary.
Treat recent group A streptococcal infection and arrange secondary penicillin prophylaxis plus cardiology assessment.
Start anticoagulation universally to prevent mitral valve thrombosis.
Perform elective valve replacement in every child with mild MR.
Prescribe antiviral therapy for rheumatic carditis.
explanations: Acute rheumatic fever with carditis requires eradication and long-term secondary prevention.
Correct: prevent recurrent GAS-triggered attacks and monitor valvular disease.
Anticoagulation is not standard unless separate indication exists.
Severity dictates surgical need; many cases are managed medically.
ARF is immune-mediated after GAS infection, not viral myocarditis.
pearl: Jones criteria use major/minor findings plus evidence of preceding streptococcal infection; carditis changes long-term follow-up.
pivot: Isolated post-streptococcal reactive arthritis may require different duration of prophylaxis and cardiology evaluation.

steps: Confirm
Jones criteria, prior GAS evidence, echo and ECG, inflammatory markers.
Treat
Eradicate GAS with appropriate penicillin regimen; control arthritis and heart failure if present.
Prevent recurrence
Secondary antibiotic prophylaxis duration by carditis/valve involvement and regional guideline.
Follow
Cardiology surveillance, education on sore-throat evaluation and adherence.
management.safety: Prophylaxis needs to continue for years; exact duration varies with residual valve disease.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

stem: A 4-year-old refuses to bear weight on the left leg with fever 39.1°C, CRP 105 mg/L and significant pain with passive hip rotation. Ultrasound shows a hip effusion. He looks systemically unwell.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate next management?
options: Diagnose transient synovitis and give NSAIDs alone without review.
Obtain urgent orthopaedic assessment for aspiration/drainage and empiric IV antibiotics after feasible cultures.
Start a month of oral prednisolone because inflammation is high.
Perform a routine growth chart review before assessing the joint.
Discharge because transient synovitis is the most common cause of limping.
explanations: Fever, inability to bear weight and marked inflammation strongly suggest septic arthritis.
Correct: septic hip can destroy cartilage and cause sepsis, requiring prompt source control.
Steroids without infection control may worsen septic arthritis.
Growth matters in paediatrics but not before an infected joint emergency.
Common does not mean safe when Kocher-type high-risk features are present.
pearl: An irritable hip with fever and inability to weight-bear is septic arthritis until excluded.
pivot: A playful afebrile child after viral illness with normal CRP and full weight-bearing may have transient synovitis.

steps: Stabilise
IV access, assess sepsis and give analgesia; blood cultures.
Sample / control
Urgent hip aspiration and surgical washout under paediatric orthopaedics.
Antibiotics
Early empiric IV therapy after rapid cultures where feasible; target organism when identified.
Protect mobility
Physiotherapy and follow-up for avascular necrosis/growth issues.
management.safety: Do not delay antimicrobials for aspiration if the child is septic or unstable.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

stem: A 2-year-old has not developed meaningful words, does not consistently respond to her name and prefers lining up toys. She makes limited eye contact but hears television advertisements from another room. Parents are concerned about autism.
options: Diagnose autism immediately without hearing assessment because she can hear TV.
Refer for comprehensive developmental assessment including formal audiology, language and social-communication assessment.
Delay referral until age five because toddlers often speak late.
Start methylphenidate to improve attention and speech.
Reassure that repetitive play is universal and no assessment is indicated.
explanations: Response to sound does not exclude partial hearing loss; ASD assessment needs broad developmental evaluation.
Correct: speech delay and social differences need evaluation for ASD and hearing/language impairment.
Early identification and interventions are beneficial.
Stimulants are not a treatment for autism-related communication delay.
Combined social/communication concerns and repetitive behaviour warrant evaluation.
pearl: Hearing loss, developmental language disorder and ASD can overlap; formal hearing testing is a key part of assessment.
pivot: If a child has normal social reciprocity and isolated articulation difficulty, language disorder may be more likely.

steps: Screen development
Communication, social reciprocity, play, motor, adaptive skills, regression and family history.
Investigate hearing
Audiology even if child reacts to loud or preferred sounds.
Support early
Speech-language therapy and early intervention while multidisciplinary ASD assessment proceeds.
Support family
Explain uncertainty without stigma, monitor co-occurring conditions.
management.safety: Loss of previously acquired skills warrants more urgent developmental/neurological assessment.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.

stem: A 4-year-old has periorbital swelling and ascites after a respiratory infection. Urine protein 4+, serum albumin 18 g/L, creatinine normal, BP 98/60 mmHg and no haematuria. He is alert with good perfusion.
ask: Which initial treatment is MOST appropriate?
options: Begin a paediatric nephrotic syndrome corticosteroid regimen after appropriate evaluation and carefully assess fluid status.
Administer an aggressive IV fluid bolus to all oedematous children.
Give antibiotics alone for presumed post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Perform routine kidney biopsy before any treatment in every typical preschool presentation.
Treat with anticoagulation for all nephrotic children irrespective of risk.
explanations: Correct: typical childhood nephrotic syndrome is often steroid-responsive minimal-change disease.
Oedema does not necessarily mean intravascular depletion; excess fluid risks pulmonary overload.
Massive proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia without haematuria/hypertension suggest nephrotic syndrome.
Biopsy is not always required initially in typical steroid-sensitive-age presentation.
Nephrosis increases thrombosis risk but anticoagulation is individualised.
pearl: Nephrotic syndrome = heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema; always assess effective circulation, infection and thrombosis risks.
pivot: If hypertension, gross haematuria, low complement or kidney impairment occur, investigate atypical nephritic or secondary causes.

steps: Assess
BP, urine protein quantification, serum albumin, renal function, infection and intravascular state.
Treat typical disease
Paediatric nephrology-guided prednisolone protocol; salt balance and diuretics only after careful assessment.
Monitor
Urine protein, weight, infection, thrombosis, renal function and steroid effects.
Teach caregivers
Relapse detection and when to seek urgent care for fever, pain, low urine.
management.safety: Severe intravascular depletion can coexist with oedema; check perfusion before diuresis.
management.local: Educational summary. Paediatric thresholds, doses and resuscitation procedures must follow local age-/weight-based policies.
